en: The Shorter Exposition:
The Exposition of the Chapter on the Way to the Far Shore;
The Exposition of the Questions.
7. The Exposition of the Questions of the Young Brahmin Nanda:
"There are sages in the world," [said the Venerable Nanda].
People speak thus: "How is this?
They say that the sage is endowed with knowledge;
or rather, is he indeed endowed with life?
“There are sages in the world.
“Are” means they exist, are present, are found, and are encountered.
“In the world” refers to the world of the lower realms (*apāya*), and so forth, up to the world of the sense bases (*āyatana*).
"Munis" refers to those named munis: the Ājīvakas, the Nigaṇṭhas, the Jaṭilas, and the ascetics (tāpasas).
People in the world perceive these as munis, yet they are not true munis.
There are, however, true munis in the world.
"Thus the Venerable Nanda.
"Thus" (*iccā*) is a euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*)... [etc. ...
"Venerable" (*āyasmā*) is a term of endearment... [etc. ...
“Nanda” is the name of that brahmin... [as before] ...the utterance—thus it was said by the Venerable Nanda.
“People say this; how is that so?”
Khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, those gone forth, devas, and humans know it.
They "declare" means they speak, utter, illuminate, and communicate. "How is this?

is a question born of doubt, a question born of perplexity, a question born of uncertainty, a question of multiple alternatives—"Is it thus? Is it not thus? What is it? How is it?"—thus [they inquire].
"People say this; how so?
'They call us a sage endowed with knowledge.

They speak of, describe, declare, illuminate, and designate the sage as one who is possessed of, fully possessed of, attained to, fully attained to, endowed with, fully endowed with, and equipped with the knowledge of the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭha-samāpatti*) or the knowledge of the five higher knowledges (*pañca-abhiññā*)."
"Do they call a sage one endowed with knowledge?

Or do they call him one endowed with life? Or rather, do they call a sage one who is possessed of, fully possessed of, has attained, fully attained, is endowed with, fully endowed with, and has acquired a life that is austere and devoted to performing many various kinds of supreme hardships?"
“They speak, they say, they illuminate, they express”—
is it indeed because one has obtained life?
Therefore that brahmin said:
“There are sages in the world,” (said the Venerable Nanda),
“thus do people speak; how is this so?”
"Do they say that a sage is endowed with knowledge,
or rather that he is endowed with life?
"Neither by view, nor by hearsay, nor by knowledge..."
The sages say that those who rejoice in the wholesome—
having cast off enmity, being free from affliction,
and devoid of longing— are called "sages."
"Neither by view, nor by hearing, nor by knowledge.
"Neither by view" means not by purification through what has been seen.
"Neither by hearing" means not by purification through what has been heard.
"Neither by knowledge"— neither by the knowledge of the eight meditative attainments, nor by the knowledge of the five higher knowledges,
nor by false knowledge— "neither by view, nor by hearsay,
nor by knowledge," O Nanda, do the wise here call one a sage.
"Skilled" means those who are skilled in the aggregates, skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense bases, skilled in dependent origination, skilled in the foundations of mindfulness,

skilled in the right efforts, skilled in the bases of psychic power, skilled in the faculties, skilled in the powers, skilled in the factors of enlightenment, skilled in the path, skilled in the fruits,
and skilled in Nibbāna— whether through purity of what is seen, purity of what is heard, or through the knowledge of the eight attainments.

They do not speak of, do not talk about, do not say, do not illuminate, and do not describe the Sage as one who is endowed, fully endowed, possessed of, fully possessed of, arrived at, fully arrived at, attained to, and fully attained to either the knowledge of the five super-knowledges,
or wrong knowledge, or what is seen, or what is heard.
"O Sage, those who are skilled say 'rejoice.
Those who wander having become detached from the world, free from distress, and free from longing—them I call 'sages' (munis).
Here, "army" refers to Māra’s army; bodily misconduct is Māra’s army, verbal misconduct is Māra’s army, and mental misconduct is Māra’s army.
The army of Māra: lust is the army of Māra, hatred is the army of Māra, delusion is the army of Māra;

anger … ill-will … contempt … insolence … envy … avarice … deceit … guile … obstinacy … aggression … conceit … arrogance … vanity … negligence … all defilements, all misconducts, all distresses, all fevers.
All unwholesome volitional formations are torments; they are Māra’s army.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Sensual pleasures are your first army...”
The second is called discontent;
the third is hunger and thirst for you,
and the fourth is said to be craving.
The fifth is sloth and torpor for you;
the sixth is called fear;
the seventh is doubt for you.
Deceit and stubbornness are your eighth;
gain, fame, honor,
and that reputation acquired through wrong means.
He who exalts himself and despises others— this,
Namuci, is your army.
It overcomes the dark one; no coward conquers it,
but having conquered it, one obtains happiness.

Because by means of the four noble paths, the entire army of Māra and all the defilements that act as adversaries have been conquered, defeated, broken, shattered, and turned away, they are therefore called "having made them foeless" (*visenikatvā*).

As for "unafflicted" (*anīghā*): lust is an affliction, hatred is an affliction, delusion is an affliction, anger is an affliction, resentment is an affliction... [and so on] ...all unwholesome volitional formations are afflictions.
Those in whom these afflictions have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and tranquillized, being incapable of arising again and burnt up by the fire of knowledge—they are called "unafflicted."
“Free from longing”: here “longing” (āsā) is said to be craving (taṇhā).
It is lust, infatuation … [as above] … ignorance, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.

Those for whom this hope and craving has been abandoned, utterly cut off, stilled, and subsided—rendered incapable of arising again and consumed by the fire of knowledge—they are called the Arhats, the ones free from longing whose taints are destroyed.
"Having become detached, free from distress, and free from longing, those who move about them I call sages.

Those who, having indeed become detached, are free from distress and free from longing, who move about, dwell, conduct themselves, behave, protect, preserve, and maintain themselves—they, in this world...

"I say they are sages"—I declare, I teach, I define, I establish, I reveal, I analyze, I clarify, and I make manifest—those who wander having become free from enmity, free from distress, and free from longing; them I call sages.
Thus said the Blessed One.
“Neither by view, nor by hearsay, nor by knowledge do the sages here,
O Nanda, declare one to be skilled;
having become free from enmity, free from affliction, and free from longing, [they are so declared].”
"Those who wander, them I call sages," said the Venerable Nanda regarding those ascetics and brahmins who exist here.
They say purification comes through what is seen and heard;
they say purification comes through rules and observances;
they speak of purification in many different ways.
"Will those who, practicing with restraint there, have crossed over birth and old age, O Blessed One?
I ask you this, Blessed One; please tell me."
“Whatever recluses and brahmins there may be”:
“whatever” (*ye keci*) is a term that encompasses everything in every way, entirely, without remainder, and exhaustively;
such is the meaning of “whatever.”
"Ascetics" (samaṇa) refers to whoever has gone forth outside of this [teaching], having entered the state of a wandering mendicant (paribbājaka).
"Brahmins" (brāhmaṇa) refers to whoever are those who address others with the title "Sir" (bhovādika)— these are the ascetics and brahmins.
"Thus the Venerable Nanda.
"Thus" (*iccā*) is a euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*)... [etc. ...
"Venerable" (*āyasmā*) is a term of endearment... [etc. ...
"Nanda" is the name of that brahmin... [as before] ...the designation—
thus the Venerable Nanda.

They say that purity comes through what is seen and heard: they speak, declare, utter, illuminate, and express that purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation come through what is seen;
they speak, declare, utter, illuminate, and express that purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation come through what is heard;

and they speak, declare, utter, illuminate, and express that purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation come through both what is seen and what is heard.
They say that purity comes through what is seen or heard;

they say that purity comes through rules and observances. They speak, declare, assert, illuminate, and employ the term "purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation" on account of moral conduct (*sīla*);

they likewise speak, declare, assert, illuminate, and employ the term "purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation" on account of rules and observances (*vata*).
They say, speak, declare, proclaim, and express purification, cleansing, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation even through rules and observances;
thus, "they say purification even through rules and observances.

They say purification in manifold ways: they say, speak, declare, proclaim, and express purification, cleansing, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation through various kinds of curious rites and auspicious ceremonies; thus...
“They speak of purification in many ways.
Might they, O Blessed One, be practicing rightly therein?
“Might they” (*kaccissu*) is a question of doubt, a question of perplexity, a question of uncertainty, a question of indecision; it is: “Is it thus? Is it not thus? What is it? How is it?”
"Kaccissu te" refers to those who hold wrong views.
"Bhagavā" is a designation for reverence... [and so on] ...it is a realization-based designation, namely, "the Blessed One."
"May they be well, O Blessed One, as they conduct themselves therein. "Therein" means:
by means of their own views, their own inclinations, their own preferences, and their own tenets.
"Restrained" means restrained, prepared, guarded, protected, preserved,
and self-controlled. "Wandering" means wandering, dwelling, moving about, conducting oneself, maintaining,
sustaining, and living— O Blessed One, were they indeed restrained while wandering there?
"Atāru jātiñca jarañca, mārisa" means: "They have crossed over, transcended, leaped over, surmounted, and passed beyond birth and aging, O venerable one.
"Mārisa" is a term of endearment, a term of respect; it is an expression used for those who possess reverence and deference—thus, "mārisa."
"I have crossed over birth and old age, dear sir.
I ask you, Blessed One: speak to me.
"I ask you" means: I ask you, I entreat you, I beseech you; "speak to me"—thus I ask you.
"Bhagavā" ... [as before] ...
is a realization-designation, namely, "Bhagavā.
"Tell me" means: tell, declare, teach, designate, establish, reveal, analyze, make plain, and explain.
“I ask you, Blessed One, please tell me this.
Thus that brahmin said:
“Whatever ascetics and brahmins there may be...”
(Thus spoke the Venerable Nanda:
"Some say purification comes through what is seen or heard;
others say purification comes through rules and observances."
They speak of purity in many ways.
O Blessed One, have those who practice with self-restraint therein crossed over birth and old age, O Venerable Sir?
“I ask you, Blessed One, please tell me this.
“Whosoever these recluses and brahmins may be,” said the Blessed One, “they [say], ‘Delight...’”
They say purification comes through what is seen and heard;
they say purification comes through rules and observances;
they say purification comes in many different ways.
"Even though they live there with restraint,
I say they have not transcended birth and old age—
those who are these ascetics and brahmins."
"Whosoever" (*ye kecīti*) is a term that exhaustively includes everything in every way, entirely, without remainder, and without exception.
"Ascetics" (*samaṇā*) refers to those who have gone forth outside of this [teaching], having entered the state of wanderers.
"Brāhmaṇas" refers to those who address others as "friend"—
that is, whatever recluses and brāhmaṇas there may be.
"Nanda" refers to the Blessed One.
"Nanda," the Blessed One addresses that brahmin by name.
"Blessed One" (bhagavā) is a designation for veneration... [as before] ...it is a descriptive term based on realization, namely "Blessed One"—thus says the Blessed One: "Nanda."

They say that purity comes through what is seen and heard: they speak, declare, utter, illuminate, and express that through what is seen there is purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation;

and they say that through what is heard there is purity … [and so on] … they say, speak, declare, utter, illuminate, and express that through both what is seen and heard there is purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation.
They say purification comes through what is seen and heard;

they say purification comes through rules and observances. By "through virtue" they mean they speak, declare, state, illuminate, and employ the terms purification, cleansing, complete cleansing, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation;
by "through observances" they likewise speak, declare, state, illuminate, and employ the term purification... [and so on].
They speak, declare, say, illuminate, and express purification, purity, complete purity, liberation, deliverance, and total deliverance even by means of rules and observances;
thus, "they speak of purification by rules and observances.

They speak of purification in manifold ways: they speak, declare, say, illuminate, and express purification, purity, complete purity, liberation, deliverance, and total deliverance by means of various kinds of curious rites and auspicious ceremonies; thus...
“They speak of purity in many ways, even though they live restrained therein. As for the phrase “even though” (*kiñcāpi*):
it is a conjunction of words, a meeting of words, a completion of words, a combination of syllables, a smoothness of phonemes, and a sequential order of words.
"Kiñcāpi" means "even though.
"Te" refers to those who hold views.
"Tattha" means with their own view, their own inclination, their own preference, and their own conviction.
"Restrained" means restrained, prepared, guarded, protected, preserved, and self-controlled.
"They move about" means they move about, dwell, conduct themselves, carry out their duties, protect, maintain, sustain, and support themselves—
even though they move about there restrained.

“They have not crossed over birth and aging,” I say, meaning that they have not crossed over, have not emerged from, have not leaped over, have not transcended, and have not passed beyond birth, aging, and death;
they have not departed from, have not escaped from, have not gone beyond, have not transcended, and have not passed beyond birth, aging, and death.
They revolve within birth, aging, and death; they revolve within the path of saṃsāra.
"Followed by birth, pursued by aging, overcome by illness, and struck down by death; without protection, without shelter, without refuge,
and having become without refuge— I say this, I declare, I teach, I establish, I set forth, I disclose, I analyze,
I make plain, and I reveal."
I say they have not transcended birth and aging.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Whatever recluses and brahmins there may be...”
(The Blessed One rejoices:
They say that purity comes through what is seen and heard;
they say that purity comes through rules and observances.
They proclaim purity in many ways; yet,
even though they conduct themselves with restraint therein,
I say they have not crossed over birth and old age.
"Whatever recluses and brahmins there may be," (said the Venerable Nanda),
"who claim purity on the basis of what has been seen or heard;"
They say purification comes through rules and observances;
they say purification comes in many forms.
If you call those sages ones who have not crossed the flood, [then what do you call those who have?].
Now, who indeed in the world of gods and humans has crossed over birth and old age, O Blessed One?
I ask you this; please tell me.
"Whatever recluses and brahmins there may be":
"whatever" (*ye keci*) is a term that encompasses everything in every way, all in all, without remainder, without exception, and exhaustively;
such is the meaning of "whatever."
"Ascetics" refers to those who have gone forth outside of this [teaching], having entered the state of wandering mendicants.
"Brahmins" refers to those who address others as "venerable sir"—
these are the ascetics and brahmins.
"Thus the Venerable Nanda.
"Thus" (*iccā*) is a phonetic conjunction (*padasandhi*) ... [etc] ...
thus the Venerable Nanda.

"They say that purity comes through what is seen and heard": they speak, declare, state, illuminate, and express that purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation come through what is seen; and they speak, declare, state, illuminate, and express that purity...
[as above] ...comes through what is heard;

and they speak, declare, state, illuminate, and express that purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation come through both what is seen and what is heard.
They say that purity comes through what is seen and heard;

they say that purity comes through rules and observances. They speak, declare, assert, proclaim, and communicate that purity, cleansing, complete purification, liberation, deliverance, and total release come through moral conduct (*sīla*);
they likewise speak, declare, assert, proclaim, and communicate that purity comes through rules and observances (*vata*).
They say, speak, utter, illuminate, and declare purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation even through rules and observances (*sīlabbata*);
thus, "they say purity even through rules and observances.

They say purity in manifold ways; they say, speak, utter, illuminate, and declare purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation through various kinds of curious rites and auspicious ceremonies; thus...
They proclaim purity in many ways. If you say of them,
"O Sage, they have not crossed over the flood," then "they" refers to those who hold to views.
"Muni": "Mona" is said to be knowledge... [as above] ...having transcended the snare of attachment, he is a muni.

When you say, "one who has not crossed the flood," you mean one who has not crossed, has not surmounted, has not overcome, and has not passed beyond the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance;
one who remains within birth, aging, and death; one who revolves within the path of saṃsāra; and one who is pursued by birth.
When one is pursued by old age, overcome by disease, struck down by death, without protection, without shelter, without refuge, and having become one who has no refuge—
if you say, "Speak," "Speak," meaning you explain, teach, set forth, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, manifest, and proclaim— then, O Sage,
you speak of those who have not crossed over the flood.
"Then who indeed in the world of gods and humans has crossed over birth and old age, O Venerable Sir?"— that is to say,
who in this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins,
its gods and humans, has crossed over, transcended, leaped over, surmounted, and passed beyond birth, old age, and death?
“‘Mārisa’ is a term of endearment, a term of respect, a synonym for one who possesses reverence and deference.
So who, indeed, in the world of gods and humans, has crossed over birth and old age, O Mārisa?
I ask you, Blessed One, please tell me.”
"I ask you" means: I ask you, I entreat you, I beseech you, I propitiate you.
"Bhagavā" is a term of reverence... [as before] ...it is a designation based on realization, namely, "Bhagavā.
"Tell me" means: tell, declare, teach, describe, establish, reveal, analyze, make plain, and explain.
“I ask you, Blessed One, please tell me this.
Therefore, that brahmin said:
“Whosoever these ascetics and brahmins may be...”
(Thus spoke the Venerable Nanda:
"Some say purification comes through what is seen or heard;
others say purification comes through rules and observances."
They speak of purity in many ways.
If you say that those sages have not crossed over the flood,
then who indeed in the world of gods and humans has?
“Mārisa, he has crossed over birth and old age;
I ask you, Blessed One, please tell me this.
“I do not say that all ascetics and brahmins [have done so].”
(The Blessed One rejoices:
"I say that those who are shrouded by birth and old age have not seen,
nor heard, nor perceived here."
Having abandoned all rules and observances,
and having abandoned all manifold forms,
they have fully understood craving and are free from taints.
"Those indeed, Nanda, I call men who have crossed the flood.
I do not say that all ascetics and brahmins are shrouded by birth and old age;
I do not, Nanda, say that all ascetics and brahmins are enveloped, shrouded, hemmed in, obstructed, and covered by birth and old age."
"I say that there are those recluses and brahmins for whom birth and aging-and-death have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump,
obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising; thus do I declare, thus do I teach, thus do I point out, thus do I establish,
thus do I reveal, thus do I analyze, thus do I clarify, thus do I make plain, thus do I manifest."
“I do not say that all ascetics and brahmins are shrouded by birth and old age, Nanda,” said the Blessed One.

“But those here who have abandoned everything—whether what is seen, heard, or sensed, or even rules and observances; those who have abandoned, relinquished, forsaken, dispelled, brought to an end, and rendered non-existent all purifications through seeing, and likewise all purifications through hearing...”
Those who have abandoned all purifications by what is heard,
those who have abandoned all purifications by what is seen, heard, or sensed, and those who have abandoned all purifications by virtue;
"Those who, having abandoned all purifications by vows,
having abandoned, relinquished, discarded, eliminated, and brought to non-existence all purifications by rules and observances"—
that is, those who have here abandoned everything seen, heard, or sensed, as well as every rule and observance.
"Having abandoned all manifold forms": having abandoned, relinquished, renounced, dispelled, brought to an end, and caused to cease all that is called purity,
purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation through various kinds of superstitious omens and auspicious rites—
this is "having abandoned all manifold forms."
"Having fully understood craving, they are free from taints; those indeed are the people who have crossed the flood, so I say.
Craving means craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena.
"Having fully understood craving" means having thoroughly understood craving by means of the three kinds of full understanding.
Through full understanding as the known, through full understanding as investigation, and through full understanding as abandonment.
What is full understanding as the known?

One knows craving: "This is craving for forms, this is craving for sounds, this is craving for odors, this is craving for tastes, this is craving for tangibles, this is craving for mental phenomena"—thus one knows and sees.
This is full understanding through knowledge.
What is full understanding through scrutiny?
Having thus known it, one scrutinizes craving as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor... [and so on].
One brings it to its conclusion by way of escape; this is the full understanding of scrutinization.
What is the full understanding of abandoning?
Having investigated in this way, one abandons craving, dispels it, brings it to an end, and causes it to cease.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, whatever desire and lust there is for craving, abandon that."
"In this way, that craving will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future.
This is the full understanding of abandoning.
"Having fully understood craving" means having fully understood craving by means of these three kinds of full understanding.
"Free from taints" means: there are four taints—the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance.

Those in whom these taints have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are subject to non-arising in the future—they are called "taintless ones," the Arahants whose taints are exhausted.
"Having fully understood craving, they are free from taints.

Those men, I say, have crossed the flood. Those who, having fully understood craving, are free from taints—they have crossed the flood of sensual desire, crossed the flood of existence, crossed the flood of views, and crossed the flood of ignorance;
they have crossed the entire path of saṃsāra; they have emerged, they have gone beyond.
"I say they have transcended, surpassed, and passed beyond; I declare, I teach, I prescribe, I establish, I reveal, I analyze, I make plain, and I illuminate them.
Those who, having fully understood craving, are free from taints—those indeed I call people who have crossed the flood."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Not all recluses and brahmins,
[said the Blessed One], do I praise.”
I say they are shrouded by birth and old age—
those who here have not abandoned everything seen, heard, or sensed, nor even all rules and observances.
Having abandoned all manifold forms and having fully understood craving, those who are free from taints—
them indeed I call people who have crossed the flood.
I rejoice in these words of the Great Seer,
so well-spoken by Gotama and free from substrate;
those who here [regard] what is seen, heard, or sensed—
Having abandoned all rules and observances,
and having abandoned all manifold forms,
they have fully understood craving and are free from taints.
"I too say that I have crossed the flood.
"I rejoice in these words of the Great Seer.

Regarding this: I rejoice in, greatly rejoice in, delight in, approve of, desire, accept, aspire for, long for, and yearn for your speech, your expression, your teaching, your instruction, and what has been taught.
"Mahesi": why is the Blessed One called "Mahesi"?
Because he sought, searched for, and pursued the great aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*), he is a "Great Seer" (*mahesi*)... [and so on] ...
"Where is the Bull among Men?"—"The Great Seer"—thus he is called.
I rejoice in these words of the Great Seer:
"Well-expounded, Gotama, is that which is without substrate.
"Well-expounded" means well-proclaimed, well-declared, well-taught, well-defined, well-established, well-unveiled, well-analyzed, well-made plain, and well-illuminated.
"Gotama, 'free from acquisitions'— here, 'acquisitions' refer to defilements, aggregates, and volitional formations. The abandoning of acquisitions, the stilling of acquisitions,
the relinquishing of acquisitions, the subsiding of acquisitions— the deathless Nibbāna—
this is well-proclaimed as 'free from acquisitions,' O Gotama."

"Having abandoned all"—that is, having abandoned, cast off, relinquished, dispelled, brought to an end, and rendered non-existent, all purifications through what is seen, heard, or sensed, as well as all rules and observances. Having abandoned all purifications through what is heard...
[and so on]... having abandoned all purifications through what is sensed... [and so on].
Whatever purities there are regarding what is seen, heard, and sensed;
whatever purities there are regarding moral conduct;
whatever purities there are regarding vows...
"Those who, having abandoned, cast off, relinquished, dispelled, brought to an end, and rendered non-existent all purifications of rules and observances (*sīlabbata*)—
those who here have abandoned everything seen, heard, or sensed, as well as every rule and observance;

who have abandoned all that is of manifold forms"— this means they have abandoned the purification, cleansing, and total purity [thought to come] from various kinds of superstitious rites and auspicious ceremonies.

"Having abandoned, cast off, relinquished, discarded, dispelled, brought to an end, and rendered non-existent liberation, release, and complete deliverance—even having abandoned all that is manifold in form;
having fully understood craving, you are free from taints. I too say of you: 'You have crossed over the flood.'"
"Craving" means craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena.
"Having fully understood craving" means having fully understood craving by means of the three kinds of full understanding:
full understanding as the known, full understanding as investigation, and full understanding as abandonment.
What is full understanding through knowing?

One knows craving: "This is craving for forms; this is craving for sounds; this is craving for odors; this is craving for tastes; this is craving for tangibles; this is craving for mental phenomena"—thus one knows and sees.
This is full understanding through knowledge. What is full understanding by scrutinization?
Having thus known it, one scrutinizes craving as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as a calamity, and as an affliction.
As alien, as subject to dissolution, as a plague, as a calamity, as a terror, as a misfortune, as unstable, as fragile,

as impermanent, as non-refuge, as non-shelter, as non-protection, as having become a non-protection, as empty, as vain, as void, as selfless, as fraught with danger, as subject to change, as coreless, as the root of evil,
as a murderer, as destruction, as accompanied by taints, as conditioned, as the bait of Māra, and as subject to birth.
One scrutinizes [them] as subject to aging, subject to illness, subject to death, subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
as subject to defilement; and as to their origin, their passing away, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them—this is the full understanding through scrutiny.
What is full understanding as abandonment?
Having investigated in this way, one abandons craving, dispels it, brings it to an end, and causes it to cease—
this is full understanding as abandonment.
"Having fully understood craving" means having thoroughly known craving by means of these three kinds of full understanding.
"Taintless" refers to the four taints:
the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance.

"Those whose taints (*āsava*) have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are subject to non-arising in the future—they are called 'taintless ones,' Arahants whose taints are exhausted.
Having fully understood craving, they are taintless; I too say that I have crossed over the flood among those who are taintless.
"I too say that I have crossed over the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, and the flood of views, among those who, having fully understood craving, are taintless."
"Crossed over the flood of ignorance, crossed over the entire path of saṃsāra, crossed over, gone beyond, reached the further shore,
transcended, and passed beyond— I say, I declare,
that having fully understood craving, they are free from taints; I too say that they have crossed the flood."
Therefore that brahmin said:
"I delight in these words of the Great Seer;
well-proclaimed, O Gotama, is that which is free from substrate."
Having abandoned whatever has been seen, heard, or sensed,
as well as all rules and observances,
and having abandoned everything in its many forms—
“Having fully understood craving and being free from taints,
I too declare that I have crossed over the flood.
Thus ends the seventh exposition, the Inquiry of the Young Brahmin Nanda.
